overview:
The Marshall Islands are 29 coral atolls and five single islands scattered across the central Pacific, with a total land area of only about 181 km², roughly the size of Washington, DC, spread over nearly two million square kilometers of ocean. The capital, Majuro, sits on an atoll so narrow that in places the road has the open ocean on one side and a calm lagoon on the other.

About 42,000 people live in the Marshall Islands. Marshallese and English are the official languages. The country is a republic in free association with the United States, an agreement that lets Marshallese live and work in the US while the US takes responsibility for defense; many Marshallese have moved to America. Coconut products, fishing licenses and a ship registry support the economy. With land averaging about two meters above sea level, rising seas and flooding are pressing everyday concerns.
landAndNature: The atolls are rings of coral reef and sandy islets enclosing lagoons, some of them enormous: Kwajalein's lagoon is among the largest in the world, over 2,000 km² of sheltered water. Soil is thin, so coconut palms, pandanus and breadfruit provide most crops and the sea provides most food. Reefs teem with reef sharks, giant clams and hundreds of coral species, and the lagoon at Bikini holds sunken warships now overgrown with coral. High tides increasingly wash across roads and into homes, and the salt spoils the freshwater lenses and taro pits that islanders have always depended on.
peopleAndCulture: Marshallese navigators were among the finest sailors in history, reading the way ocean swells bend around islands and teaching those patterns with stick charts, lattices of palm ribs and shells that mapped waves rather than coastlines. Outrigger canoes are still sailed and raced. Weavers turn pandanus leaves into fine mats, baskets and fans. Meals center on fish, breadfruit, coconut and rice, and community feasts often follow church services, since most Marshallese are Christian. A kemem, the party for a child's first birthday, is the biggest family celebration, with singing and enough food for a whole village. Basketball and volleyball are favorite sports.
history: Voyagers settled these atolls around 2,000 years ago and developed remarkable navigation skills. Spain claimed the islands, Germany bought them in 1885, and Japan took them during World War I. Fierce fighting between Japanese and American forces swept the atolls in 1944. From 1946 to 1958 the United States tested 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak, including the very large Castle Bravo test of 1954; communities were moved off their home islands, some people were exposed to fallout, and parts of those atolls remain unsafe to live on. The Marshall Islands became self-governing in 1979 and fully independent in 1986 under a compact with the United States.
funFacts: Marshallese navigators made stick charts from palm ribs and shells to teach how ocean swells bend around islands.
Kwajalein Atoll encloses one of the largest lagoons in the world, wider than the land area of many countries.
Sixty-seven nuclear weapons were tested at Bikini and Enewetak between 1946 and 1958, and some areas remain unsafe.
The two-piece swimsuit called the bikini was named after Bikini Atoll shortly after the first test there in 1946.
The country's land averages about two meters above the sea, so high tides can wash straight across the roads.
